reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Classic triad of iron-deficiency anaemia, dysphagia, and upper (post-cricoid) oesophageal webs
Most often affects middle-aged women and is now uncommon where iron deficiency is well managed
Dysphagia is typically to solids and results from the cervical web narrowing the lumen
Associated features include glossitis, angular cheilitis, koilonychia, and other signs of chronic iron deficiency
Recognised as a premalignant condition with an increased risk of post-cricoid and upper oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma
Cornerstone of management is iron repletion, which often improves the dysphagia, with endoscopic dilatation for persistent webs
Long-term surveillance is warranted given the malignant potential
reference.pathophysiology: Plummer-Vinson syndrome links chronic iron deficiency to the formation of upper oesophageal webs and dysphagia. Iron deficiency is thought to impair the turnover of the rapidly dividing oesophageal mucosa and reduce iron-dependent oxidative enzymes, leading to mucosal atrophy and web formation in the post-cricoid region. The web mechanically narrows the lumen, causing solid-food dysphagia, while the chronic atrophic and inflammatory changes are believed to underlie the increased long-term risk of squamous carcinoma of the hypopharynx and upper oesophagus.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with iron studies confirming iron-deficiency anaemia
Barium swallow demonstrating a post-cricoid web
Upper endoscopy with biopsy to confirm the web and exclude malignancy
Investigation for the source of iron loss, including gastrointestinal blood loss
Ear-nose-throat evaluation of the hypopharynx where indicated
redFlags: Progressive dysphagia, weight loss, or hoarseness suggesting malignancy
A post-cricoid mass or ulcer on imaging or endoscopy
Occult gastrointestinal blood loss requiring source identification
reference.prognosis: Dysphagia frequently improves with iron repletion, and webs respond to dilatation; the principal long-term concern is the elevated risk of upper aerodigestive squamous carcinoma, which justifies ongoing surveillance.
pitfalls: Treating the web without correcting the underlying iron deficiency
Failing to investigate the cause of iron loss
Missing an early post-cricoid carcinoma in a patient with sideropenic dysphagia
Neglecting long-term surveillance given the premalignant nature of the condition
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease
management: Iron repletion with oral or parenteral iron is the cornerstone and frequently relieves the dysphagia
Endoscopic bougie or balloon dilatation for cervical webs that persist despite adequate iron repletion
Identify and treat the underlying source of iron loss, such as gastrointestinal blood loss or menorrhagia
Address associated iron-deficiency features including glossitis, angular cheilitis and koilonychia, and optimise dietary iron
Endoscopic surveillance of the hypopharynx and upper oesophagus given the premalignant risk of squamous carcinoma
Ear-nose-throat referral to evaluate the post-cricoid region and any suspicious mucosal change
Escalate for biopsy and oncological assessment if a mass, refractory stricture or persistent symptoms suggest malignant transformation
